title: Count the Rising Triples

concept.title: Fix the middle element: the triples through it are the smaller numbers on its left times the larger numbers on its right
body: A **rising triple** is a choice of three positions `i < j < k` with `a[i] < a[j] < a[k]`. In `1 2 3 1 4` the triples at the positions `1 2 3`, `1 2 5`, `1 3 5` and `2 3 5` rise, so there are 4. Checking all triples is O(n^3), which is hopeless for 50000 numbers.

Look at the **middle** element `j`. Any smaller number on its left can be the first element, and any larger number on its right can be the last one, independently. So the number of triples with the middle `j` is `smallerLeft[j] * largerRight[j]`, and the answer is the sum over all `j`. Both counts come from a Fenwick tree over the **ranks** of the values (numbers up to `10^9` are replaced by their rank among the distinct values).

body.code:
for j in range(n):                       # left to right
    smaller[j] = bit_sum(t, rk[j] - 1)    # earlier values below
    bit_add(t, rk[j], 1)
for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):           # right to left, a fresh tree
    larger = (n - 1 - j) - bit_sum(t2, rk[j])   # later values above
    total += smaller[j] * larger
    bit_add(t2, rk[j], 1)

body: The count of later values above is "all later values" minus "later values that are at most `a[j]`" (equal values are not larger). The answer can reach about `n^3 / 6`, which is more than 2 * 10^13 for 50000 numbers, so it needs 64-bit integers. Time O(n log n).

statement: A list of `n` numbers is given. Count the triples of positions `i < j < k` for which `a[i] < a[j] < a[k]` holds with both signs strict. Print the count.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the length of the list.
The second line has the `n` numbers of the list.
outputFormat: Print one number: the count of rising triples.

examples.note: The triples of positions (1, 2, 3), (1, 2, 5), (1, 3, 5) and (2, 3, 5) have rising values: 4.

hints: Fix the middle element of the triple.
The number of triples with the middle j is (smaller numbers before j) times (larger numbers after j).
Both counts come from a Fenwick tree over the ranks of the values, one pass from each side.

explanation: For every middle element the triples are the smaller numbers before it times the larger numbers after it. Two Fenwick passes over the ranks of the values give both counts.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

def bit_add(t, i, x):
    n = len(t) - 1
    while i <= n:
        t[i] += x
        i += i & -i

def bit_sum(t, i):
    s = 0
    while i > 0:
        s += t[i]
        i -= i & -i
    return s

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

vals = sorted(set(a))
rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
m = len(vals)
rk = [rank[v] for v in a]
smaller = [0] * n
t = [0] * (m + 1)
for j in range(n):
    smaller[j] = bit_sum(t, rk[j] - 1)
    bit_add(t, rk[j], 1)
t = [0] * (m + 1)
total = 0
for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    larger = (n - 1 - j) - bit_sum(t, rk[j])
    total += smaller[j] * larger
    bit_add(t, rk[j], 1)
print(total)
